Pure functions

Small, pure TypeScript functions for the everyday math in UI and graphics code: interpolation, easing, smoothing, seeded randomness, angles, 2D vectors, geometry and colors. No runtime dependencies. Works with ESM, CommonJS and TypeScript, and subpath imports keep your bundle small.

Install and import

Root, one namespace per module01

import { math, easing } from '@ashwinthomas/utils';

Subpath, only what you need02

import { lerp } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/math';

CJS require03

const { math } = require('@ashwinthomas/utils');

Overview

What it is - @ashwinthomas/utils collects the small calculations that interface and graphics code keeps rewriting: keeping a value in range, mapping it from one range to another, easing, smoothing, wrapping angles, working with 2D points and converting colors. 53 functions and a Vector2 class, split into 8 modules you can import separately.

Who it's for - Front-end and creative developers working on UI animation, scroll effects, canvas or WebGL sketches, small games and charts: anywhere a number needs to be mapped, limited or smoothed from one frame to the next.

Why it stays small - Each module can be imported on its own, and importing the package doesn't run any code by itself, so your bundler keeps only the functions you use. Types are included for ESM and CommonJS, with nothing extra to install.

Conventions

A - Angles are in radians, except the inputs and outputs of degToRad/radToDeg and color hue, which uses degrees like CSS.

B - Easing functions take a progress value t from 0 to 1, and return 0 at the start and 1 at the end.

C - A 2D point or vector is a plain Vec2 = { x: number; y: number } object. Vector2 instances have the same shape, so they work with every function.

D - Functions never change their inputs and keep no state between calls. The only exception is the unseeded random functions, which use Math.random.

Playground

Every number below is calculated live by the published package, the same code you install from npm. Drag, click and slide to see how each function behaves, including at the edges.

01 / 08

math

Keep numbers in range, map them from one range to another, and round them. interpolate maps a value from one range onto another. The input range can count up or down, but it can't change direction partway; the output range can be any shape, like [0, 1, 0] to rise and fall back.

Use it for fading something in as the page scrolls, keeping a slider thumb inside its track, snapping a dragged item to a grid, and comparing decimals that are almost but not exactly equal.

clamp(value, min, max)
Keeps a value between min and max.
lerp(start, end, t)
The value a fraction t of the way from start to end. t isn't limited to 0–1.
invlerp(start, end, value)
The reverse of lerp: how far value is between start and end. Returns 0 if start and end are the same.
interpolate(value, inputRange, outputRange, extrapolate)
Maps value from one range to another. extrapolate decides what happens outside the input range: 'extend' (the default) keeps going, 'clamp' stops at the ends and 'identity' returns the value unchanged. Ranges of different lengths, or an input range that changes direction, throw a RangeError.
mod(n, d) · sign(n)
A remainder that takes the sign of d, so mod(-1, 5) is 4. sign returns −1, 0 or 1 (NaN for NaN).
roundTo(value, decimals) · snap(value, step)
Rounds to a number of decimal places without the usual floating-point slips (1.005 rounds to 1.01). Negative decimals round to tens, hundreds and so on. snap rounds to the nearest multiple of step.
near(a, b, epsilon)
True when a and b are within epsilon of each other (default 1e-6).

interpolate(150, [0, 100], [0, 1], 'extend') // 1.5

  • clamp(n, 0, 10)7.35
  • snap(n, 2.5)7.5
  • roundTo(n, 1)7.4
  • roundTo(n, -1)10
  • mod(n, 5)2.35
  • sign(n)1
  • invlerp(-20, 20, n)0.684
  • near(n, 0, 0.5)false

02 / 08

random

range gives a random number and rangeFloor a random whole number, from 0 to 1, 0 to max, or min to max. The upper limit is never returned. Both use Math.random. withSeed gives you a generator that repeats the same sequence for the same seed. Roll some samples and watch the bars even out; then type a seed and press Reset to get the exact same counts again.

Use it for jittering particles, picking a random array item with items[rangeFloor(items.length)], generative art you can recreate from a seed, and tests that need the same "random" input on every run.

range() · range(max) · range(min, max)
A random number from 0 up to 1, up to max, or from min up to max. The upper limit is never returned.
rangeFloor() · rangeFloor(max) · rangeFloor(min, max)
The same, but always a whole number.
withSeed(seed?)
A generator that repeats exactly for the same seed, with value, range and rangeFloor. The seed can be a number or a string. rng.seed holds the seed it used, so withSeed(rng.seed) plays the same sequence again.
  1. Value 0: 0
  2. Value 1: 0
  3. Value 2: 0
  4. Value 3: 0
  5. Value 4: 0
  6. Value 5: 0
  7. Value 6: 0
  8. Value 7: 0
  9. Value 8: 0
  10. Value 9: 0

03 / 08

motion

damp moves a value part of the way to its target each frame, adjusted for how much time has passed. That keeps the motion the same at 30, 60 or 144 fps. Click the track to move the target; a higher lambda gets there faster.

Use it for a camera that follows a player, a cursor that trails the pointer, or any value that should glide toward a moving target. smoothstep gives soft edges to fades, vignettes and masks.

damp(current, target, lambda, deltaTime)
Moves current toward target by an amount set by lambda and deltaTime, the time since the last frame.
smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x)
A smooth S-curve from 0 to 1 between the two edges: 0 before edge0, 1 after edge1.

x = damp(x, 80, 8, dt) // 10

04 / 08

easing

Every easing function has the same shape: type EasingFn = (t: number) => number. Pass in progress t from 0 to 1 and get back an eased value that starts at 0 and ends at 1. The Expo versions land on exactly 0 and 1, and the Back versions overshoot a little (by the standard 1.70158) before settling.

Use it for animations, progress bars and scroll effects: ease the progress first, then pass it to lerp to get the actual value.

Cubic
Speeds up and slows down gently. easeOutCubic is a good default for interface motion.
Expo
Starts or stops sharply, then takes its time, landing exactly on 0 and 1.
Back
Pulls back or overshoots slightly before settling, for motion that feels playful and physical.

easeOutBack(0.00) // 0.000

05 / 08

angle

lerpAngle blends between two angles the short way round. The dashed line is plain lerp, which takes the long way when the angles sit on either side of ±180° (±π).

Use it for turning a sprite to face where it's heading, rotating dials and knobs, and blending compass directions without a sudden spin the wrong way.

degToRad(deg) · radToDeg(rad)
Convert between degrees and radians.
normalizeAngle(rad)
Wraps any angle into the range −π to π, so 3π becomes π.
lerpAngle(a, b, t)
Blends between two angles the shorter way round.

lerpAngle(a, b, t) // 3.316 rad · -170° lerp(a, b, t) // 0.175 rad · 10°

06 / 08

vector

A vector is an arrow with a direction and a length, stored as { x, y }. Drag the tips of a and b, or focus one and use the arrow keys. One grid square is one unit, and y counts upward, like a graph on paper.

Use it for moving things by a velocity, finding which way one object should travel to reach another, and checking with dot whether two directions point the same way.

add(a, b) · subtract(a, b) · scale(v, s)
Add or subtract two vectors, or stretch one by a number. Each returns a new vector and leaves the inputs alone.
magnitude(v) · normalize(v)
A vector's length, and the same direction shortened to length 1. A zero vector normalizes to { x: 0, y: 0 }.
dot(a, b) · direction(from, to)
dot is positive when two vectors point roughly the same way, 0 at a right angle and negative when they point apart. direction is the length-1 vector from one point to another.
new Vector2(x, y) · Vector2.from(v) · Vector2.fromAngle(angle, length)
A class version of the same math. Methods like add, rotate, lerp and angleTo can be chained, and each returns a new Vector2. Instances are valid Vec2 objects, so you can pass them to any function.
  • a, b // { x: 3, y: 1 }, { x: -1, y: 1.5 }
  • add(a, b) // { x: 2, y: 2.5 }
  • subtract(a, b) // { x: 4, y: -0.5 }
  • magnitude(a) // 3.16
  • normalize(a) // { x: 0.95, y: 0.32 }
  • dot(a, b) // -1.5 · pointing apart
  • Vector2.from(a).add(b).scale(0.5) // { x: 1, y: 1.25 }

07 / 08

geometry

Drag the four points, or focus one and use the arrow keys. intersection finds where the two segments cross and returns null when they don't, including when they're parallel. Readouts count y upward, which is also the direction rotatePoint turns: counter-clockwise.

Use it for checking whether two lines cross, laying items out in a circle with polar, measuring distances, and rotating points around a pivot.

distance(a, b) · angle(from, to)
The distance between two points, and the angle from one to the other, in radians.
rotatePoint(point, angle, origin)
Turns a point counter-clockwise around origin, which defaults to { x: 0, y: 0 }.
polar(radius, angle, origin)
Turns a radius and an angle into an { x, y } point, measured from origin.
intersection(a1, a2, b1, b2)
Where two line segments cross, or null if they don't.

  • angle(a1, a2) // 0.504 rad
  • intersection(a1, a2, b1, b2) // { x: 189.07, y: 126.73 }
  • m = Vector2.from(a1).lerp(a2, 0.5) // { x: 195, y: 130 }
  • polar(24, angle(a1, a2) + π / 2, m) // { x: 183.41, y: 151.01 }
  • rotatePoint(b2, π / 2, b1) // { x: 230, y: 460 }

08 / 08

color

Convert colors between hex, RGB, HSL and HSV, mix them, lighten or darken them, and check how readable text will be. RGB values go from 0 to 255, hue is in degrees, and everything else goes from 0 to 1. Transparency (alpha) is kept through every conversion. Pick two colors to see how they blend and whether one is readable on the other.

Use it for building a range of shades from one brand color, animating from one color to another with mixColor, and checking that text has enough contrast against its background.

hexToRgb(hex) · rgbToHex(rgb)
Reads #rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb and #rrggbbaa (the # is optional) and throws a RangeError for anything else. rgbToHex writes lowercase hex and only adds alpha when it's below 1.
rgbToHsl · hslToRgb · rgbToHsv · hsvToRgb
Convert RGB to HSL or HSV and back. Hue wraps around to stay between 0 and 360, and RGB results are whole numbers.
hexToHsl(hex) · hslToHex(hsl)
Shortcuts that go through RGB for you.
mixColor(a, b, t)
Blends a toward b by t, one channel at a time. If only one color has alpha, the other counts as fully opaque.
lighten(rgb, amount) · darken(rgb, amount)
Raise or lower lightness by amount (0 to 1), without going past white or black.
luminance(rgb) · contrastRatio(a, b)
How bright a color is, from 0 (black) to 1 (white), and how readable two colors are together, from 1 (no contrast) to 21 (black on white).
  • contrastRatio(a, b) // 6.21:1 · AA pass · AA large pass · AAA fail
  • hexToRgb(a) // { r: 0, g: 79, b: 184 }
  • rgbToHsl(a) // { h: 214.2, s: 1, l: 0.36 }
  • rgbToHex(mixColor(a, b, t)) // #769dcf

Recipes

Six small patterns from the playground, ready to copy. Each imports from a subpath, so only the functions it uses end up in your bundle.

Scroll-linked fade

01

Fade a hero out over the first 400px of scrolling. 'clamp' stops the opacity going below 0 or above 1.

import { interpolate } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/math';

const hero = document.querySelector('.hero');

addEventListener('scroll', () => {
  hero.style.opacity = interpolate(scrollY, [0, 400], [1, 0], 'clamp');
}, { passive: true });

Frame-rate independent follow

02

A dot that follows the pointer smoothly, and moves the same on a 60 Hz laptop as on a 144 Hz monitor.

import { damp } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/motion';

const dot = document.querySelector('.dot');
let x = 0, target = 0, last = performance.now();
addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => { target = e.clientX; });

requestAnimationFrame(function frame(now) {
  const dt = (now - last) / 1000;
  last = now;
  x = damp(x, target, 8, dt);
  dot.style.translate = `${x}px 0`;
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
});

Eased tween

03

Turn elapsed time into progress from 0 to 1, ease it, then lerp from the start value to the end value.

import { clamp, lerp } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/math';
import { easeOutCubic } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/easing';

function tween(from, to, ms, onUpdate) {
  const start = performance.now();
  requestAnimationFrame(function step(now) {
    const t = clamp((now - start) / ms, 0, 1);
    onUpdate(lerp(from, to, easeOutCubic(t)));
    if (t < 1) requestAnimationFrame(step);
  });
}

Snap a drag to a grid

04

Round to the nearest 24px cell, then keep the result inside the canvas.

import { clamp, snap } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/math';

const CELL = 24;

function toGrid({ x, y }, width, height) {
  return {
    x: clamp(snap(x, CELL), 0, width),
    y: clamp(snap(y, CELL), 0, height),
  };
}

Readable text on any background

05

Choose white or dark text, whichever is easier to read on the background color.

import { contrastRatio, hexToRgb } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/color';

const WHITE = hexToRgb('#ffffff');
const INK = hexToRgb('#121212');

function textColorFor(background) {
  const bg = hexToRgb(background);
  return contrastRatio(bg, WHITE) >= contrastRatio(bg, INK) ? '#ffffff' : '#121212';
}

textColorFor('#004fb8'); // '#ffffff' (7.47:1 vs 2.51:1)

Reproducible generative layout

06

The same seed gives the same layout every time, so a design you like can be saved as one short string.

import { withSeed } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/random';

function scatter(seed, count, width, height) {
  const rng = withSeed(seed);
  return Array.from({ length: count }, () => ({
    x: rng.range(width),
    y: rng.range(height),
    size: rng.rangeFloor(4, 12),
  }));
}

scatter('poster-01', 40, 800, 600); // same 40 dots every run

Questions

Short answers about installing and using the package, and about the ideas behind it. Missing something? Open an issue on GitHub.

Package

What is @ashwinthomas/utils?

+

@ashwinthomas/utils is a small TypeScript library of 53 utility functions for math, randomness (including seeded), motion, easing, angles, 2D vectors, geometry and colors. It has no runtime dependencies and works with ES modules, CommonJS and TypeScript.

How do I install and import it?

+

Run npm i @ashwinthomas/utils. Importing from the package root gives you one object per module, so import { math } from '@ashwinthomas/utils' lets you call math.clamp. To import functions by name, use a module path instead: import { clamp } from '@ashwinthomas/utils/math'. CommonJS require works the same way.

Does it work in the browser and in Node.js?

+

Yes. It only uses standard JavaScript and Math, so it runs in any modern browser and in Node.js 18 or later, with either import or require.

Is it tree-shakeable?

+

Yes. Importing the package doesn't run any code by itself, and every module has its own path, such as @ashwinthomas/utils/math. Importing from those paths keeps bundles smallest. Bundlers like webpack 5 also drop unused functions when you import a module object from the root.

Does it include TypeScript types?

+

Yes. Type definitions are included for both ESM and CommonJS, including the Vec2 and EasingFn types, so your editor shows signatures and autocomplete without installing anything else.

Can I use it in commercial projects?

+

Yes. It's released under the MIT license, which lets you use, change and share it in commercial and closed-source projects, as long as you keep the copyright and license notice.

Can I seed the random functions?

+

Yes. withSeed(seed) returns a generator that gives the same sequence every time for the same seed. It's based on the mulberry32 algorithm and has value, range and rangeFloor. The seed can be a number or a string; leave it out for a random seed, then read rng.seed to save it and replay the sequence later. Don't use it for anything security-related.

Concepts

What is the difference between lerp and invlerp?

+

lerp(start, end, t) gives the value a fraction t of the way from start to end, so lerp(0, 200, 0.25) is 50. invlerp(start, end, value) goes the other way and gives you the fraction, so invlerp(0, 200, 50) is 0.25. To go from one range straight to another, use interpolate.

How is damp different from lerp?

+

Calling lerp(a, b, t) every frame moves a fixed share each frame, so the motion speeds up on faster screens. damp(current, target, lambda, deltaTime) takes the time since the last frame into account, so it moves the same at 30, 60 or 144 fps.

What is smoothstep used for?

+

smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) returns 0 below edge0, 1 above edge1, and a smooth S-curve in between. It's a common way to soften a hard cut-off, like fading something in over a scroll range or softening the edge of a mask.

Which easing function should I use?

+

For most interface motion, easeOutCubic: it starts quickly and slows down gently, which feels responsive. Use the InOut versions for movement between two resting points, Expo for sharper, more dramatic moves, and Back when a small overshoot suits the feel.

How does mod differ from the % operator?

+

JavaScript's % can return a negative number: -1 % 5 is -1. mod(n, d) always takes the sign of d, so mod(-1, 5) is 4. That's usually what you want when wrapping an index or position around a loop.

What does interpolate do with values outside the input range?

+

By default ('extend') it keeps going in the same direction, so interpolate(150, [0, 100], [0, 1]) is 1.5. 'clamp' stops at the ends of the output range, and 'identity' returns the input value unchanged.

How do I interpolate between two angles the short way?

+

Use lerpAngle(a, b, t). It always turns the shorter way, so going from 170° to −170° passes through 180° instead of turning 340° the other way. Angles are in radians; convert with degToRad first.

Why are angles in radians?

+

Radians are what Math.sin, Math.cos and Math.atan2 use, so sticking with them avoids converting back and forth. Use degToRad and radToDeg when you need degrees, for example for user input. The one exception is color hue, which is in degrees, like CSS.

How do I find where two line segments intersect?

+

Call intersection(a1, a2, b1, b2) with the end points of both segments as { x, y } objects. It returns the point where they cross, or null if they don't cross, including when they're parallel or lie along the same line.

Should I use Vector2 or the vector functions?

+

Either: both use the same { x, y } shape. The functions work on plain objects you already have. Vector2 puts the same math in a class you can chain, like new Vector2(3, 4).add({ x: 1, y: 1 }).scale(2), and every method returns a new Vector2. Instances work with the functions too, so you can mix them.

How do I check color contrast for accessibility?

+

Turn both colors into RGB with hexToRgb, then call contrastRatio(a, b). It returns a number from 1 to 21. WCAG level AA asks for at least 4.5 for normal text and 3 for large text; level AAA asks for 7. White on black is 21.

Contributing

To work on the library itself, clone the repo, then:

npm run build      # tsup → dist/
npm run dev        # tsup --watch
npm test           # vitest run
npm run test:watch # vitest
npm run typecheck  # tsc --noEmit

Requires npm 11+ to install dev dependencies (npm 10.9 crashes resolving Vitest 4's peer dependencies).
